short: Two seaborne invasions of Kyushu, both broken by storms the Japanese later called kamikaze.
full:
Kublai Khan sent envoys demanding tribute from Japan; the Kamakura shogunate did not reply. In November 1274 a fleet of some 900 ships carrying Mongol, Chinese and Korean troops overran Tsushima and Iki and landed at Hakata Bay. The fighting favoured the invaders, whose massed formations, crossbows and exploding shells suited them better than samurai single combat, but they re-embarked after a day and a storm wrecked much of the fleet on the passage home.

Japan spent the next seven years building a stone wall around Hakata Bay. The second attempt in 1281 was one of the largest amphibious operations before the twentieth century: two fleets, perhaps 4,400 vessels and 140,000 men, sailing from Korea and from newly conquered southern China. The wall held them off the beaches for weeks while small boats raided their anchorage at night. On 15 August a typhoon destroyed the fleet where it lay. The wrecks off Takashima have since been excavated. Japan read the deliverance as divine, and the term kamikaze — divine wind — dates from it.
